research_summary: Candidates: (1) What if the Moon disappeared? 34/40 (curiosity gap, personal stakes, ties to the tides documentary that promised it as the next video, strong visuals), (2) What if Earth stopped spinning? 33 (made as a Short on 18 Nov), (3) What if you fell into a black hole? 33 (used for today's documentary). Winner: the Moon; continues the 'The Moon' cluster (supermoon Short, tides documentary) and is the exact 'next video' the tides documentary asks the viewer to watch. Titles considered (/50): 'What If the Moon Disappeared Tomorrow?' 44 (chosen); 'If the Moon Vanished, Would You Notice?' 40; 'Earth Without the Moon' 36; 'The Moon Is Gone: Tides, Night, Tilt' 38; 'What Your Life Looks Like With No Moon' 39; 'The Night The Moon Disappeared' 37; 'Could Earth Survive Without the Moon?' 41; 'No Moon, No Tides?' 38; 'What the Moon Quietly Does For You' 40; 'Moonless Earth Explained' 34. Thumbnails: A Earth with an empty orbit and a ghost Moon outline, text NO MOON? (chosen); B a dark landscape night with no Moon and many stars; C a tilted Earth wobbling. Hooks: 'Tomorrow night the Moon is gone. The tides shrink to a fraction.' (chosen); 'The Moon quietly does three jobs for you. Remove it and all three fail.'; 'You would see the difference within hours.'; 'The sea would calm down tomorrow.'; 'Nights would get truly dark.' FACTS (status): the Moon's tidal effect is more than twice the Sun's, so without the Moon the remaining Sun tide is much smaller - VERIFIED (NOAA education: Sun's pull ~178x the Moon's, but the Moon's tidal pull is over twice the Sun's because it is much closer); NASA's Jim Green says tides would be 'radically reduced' without the Moon - VERIFIED (NASA, Your Moon Questions Answered); a full Moon is roughly 25-150 times brighter than a clear moonless sky - COMPUTED from published illuminance values (full Moon about 0.05-0.32 lux, clear moonless sky with airglow about 0.002 lux; sources differ and some publications cite wrong full-Moon values) - PARTIALLY VERIFIED, stated as 'dozens of times' and '25 to 150 x'; the Moon's gravity helps stabilise Earth's axial tilt / climate - VERIFIED as NASA's statement (Top Moon Questions) but PARTIALLY VERIFIED as science: a NASA-hosted moonless-Earth model finds the tilt varies more but stays within a constrained range over 100,000 years, so the script says 'could wander over a very long time' and 'Scientists think'; the Moon does not hold us on Earth, Earth's gravity does - VERIFIED (basic gravity). Sources: https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides07_cycles.html , https://science.nasa.gov/moon/top-moon-questions/ , https://www.nasa.gov/podcasts/gravity-assist/gravity-assist-podcast-your-moon-questions-answered/ , https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20140011208 , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(illuminance) . english.pinned_comment: If the Moon vanished tomorrow, which would you miss first: the moonlit nights or the ocean tides?

scenes.text: Tomorrow night the Moon is gone. The tides shrink to a fraction.
Weird, right? So what else changes? Let's find out.
First, the sea. The Moon makes more than half of our tide. Without it, only the Sun's gentle tide is left.
Now the night. A full Moon is dozens of times brighter than a moonless sky. Nights would turn truly dark.
Then the wobble. Scientists think the Moon's gravity helps keep Earth's tilt steady. Without it, the tilt could wander over a very long time.
Would we float off? No. The Moon doesn't hold you down. Earth's gravity does.
Quick quiz: what changes first? The tides and the night, right away. The tilt takes ages.
So no Moon means weaker tides, darker nights and a wobblier future. Would you miss it? Tell me below!
